tagline.text: The ancestral-home museum of the painter Juan Luna and his brother, General Antonio Luna

location.label: Location
location.text: Badoc town, Ilocos Norte, at the corner of Jose Rizal Street and Juan Luna Street

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱200~800 (per person, based on a half-day trip from Laoag including transport and meals; admission is free)

children.text: The Juan Luna Shrine in Badoc, Ilocos Norte, is a museum in the restored home of the brothers Juan Luna, the painter, Antonio Luna, the general, and Manuel Luna, the violinist. Its official name is the Juan and Antonio Luna Museum; it reopened in an expanded form in 2016 with touch screens and video exhibits, and admission is free.

The Juan Luna Shrine is the old home of the Luna family in the town of Badoc, Ilocos Norte. It is now presented as the Juan and Antonio Luna Museum, run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP), and Wikipedia describes it as a restored two-story ancestral house of the painter Juan Luna, the revolutionary general Antonio Luna and the violinist Manuel Luna. Records say Juan Luna was born in Badoc in 1857 and baptized on October 27 of that year in the nearby church. Juan and Antonio are known as two great brothers of the Philippine independence movement, and this house lets you glimpse their childhood and family life.

Here is the building's history. The original house burned in a fire in 1861 and is said to have been rebuilt with clay bricks and molave wood. According to one blog, it is an early-19th-century bahay na tisa (tile-roofed house) style; the government received the house in 1954, and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and the National Historical Institute (NHI) restored it in 1977, after which it began to be used as a museum. On April 27, 2016, the NHCP reopened the renovated and expanded museum, and NHCP chair Maria Serena Diokno is said to have led the opening. Technology exhibits such as touch-screen TVs and a projection of Antonio Luna's speaking face were added then.

The exhibits are divided into six galleries covering the life and career of Juan Luna, his studio in Paris, the life and career of Antonio Luna, the Luna home in the 19th century, Antonio's letter to Conchita Castillo, and trench warfare. On the second floor, a living room, bedrooms, an azotea (balcony) and a small chapel are furnished with period pieces, and the structure of the house itself shows the life of an old Ilocos upper-class family. However, some reviews say many exhibits are replicas. Antonio's military cap, works such as Juan's Parisian Life, a portrait and Juan's masterpiece the Spoliarium are said to be reproductions, so the originals are better seen at the National Museum in Manila and elsewhere.

The appeal of this place lies not in its size but in following a family's story. Juan made his name in Europe as a painter, and his younger brother Antonio is known to have become a general of the Philippine revolutionary army, as a soldier and a pharmacist, and to have lost his life during the war for independence. The fact that these two brothers grew up in the same house leaves visitors with a quiet resonance. Admission is free and it is small enough to see in about an hour, and paired with the nearby Badoc Church it makes a half-day route in southern Ilocos Norte. The opening days and fees here are based on blogs and NHCP-related guidance, so check before you visit.

blocks.title: The restored home of the Luna brothers

children.text: A two-story house rebuilt with clay bricks and molave wood. On the second floor, a living room, bedrooms, an azotea and a small chapel are furnished with period pieces. From the building's structure you can feel how an upper-class Ilocos family lived in the 19th century.

blocks.title: Gallery on Juan Luna's life and career

children.text: This gallery explains the painter's life and career. Reviews say many of the paintings shown are replicas, so see the originals at the National Museum in Manila.

A gallery that recreates the atmosphere of the Paris studio where Juan stayed. You can imagine the setting in which the painter worked in Europe. Check the signs on site as to whether photography is allowed.

It introduces the life of Antonio, a revolutionary general. A distinctive feature is the projected video, introduced in the 2016 expansion, in which Antonio's speaking face appears. Ask the staff on site about video showing times.
A gallery on the letter Antonio sent to Conchita Castillo. You can catch a glimpse of the human side behind his soldierly image.
A gallery that covers trench warfare. It helps you understand the style of fighting in the period when Antonio Luna was in command. Check on site what language the explanations are in.
Digital exhibits introduced in the 2016 expansion make it interesting even for children. It is a small provincial museum, but the exhibits that use technology are unexpectedly substantial.

It is close to Badoc Church, where Juan was baptized, so the two are good to see together. The church is also a shrine to the miraculous statue of the Virgin. See the Badoc Church entry for the church.

items.title: Half-day route from Laoag
items.subtitle: The Luna museum and Badoc Church

children.text: Take a bus heading south to Badoc from Laoag. It is about 39 km from Laoag, and you should check the travel time locally.
Get off in Badoc town and take a tricycle to the museum. Look at the outside of the museum and its front yard first.
NHCP museums usually open early in the morning, so enter just after opening and start with the quiet galleries. Some sources say it opens at
and others
Look around the second-floor living room, bedrooms, azotea and small chapel.
Go to nearby Badoc Church to see the statue of La Virgen Milagrosa and the church building.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town and return to Laoag.
Some guidance says the museum closes on Mondays, so avoid Mondays.

items.subtitle: Sinait Church, Badoc Church, the Luna museum

children.text: Come south from Laoag and look around Sinait Church first.
Learn the story of the Virgin statue at Badoc Church.
Have lunch in town.
Follow the story of the brothers Juan and Antonio at the Luna museum.
Look around the beach or Badoc Island, then return to Laoag.
A chartered vehicle is efficient for getting around.
There are direct flights from Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila to Laoag International Airport. Airlines and times vary by season, so check when you book.
One approach described is to take a Laoag-bound bus from Manila (Cubao), ask to be let off on the road near Badoc town, and take a tricycle from there to the museum.
It is about 445 km from Manila to Badoc. The bus ride is known to take about
9–11 hours

items.title: From Laoag or Vigan to Badoc

children.text: It lies about 39 km south of Laoag. Take a bus that runs between Laoag and Vigan and get off on the road near Badoc.
From the road to the museum in town is a short tricycle ride.
One guide describes Badoc as about halfway between Vigan and Laoag.
The museum and Badoc Church are close to each other. Walk or take a tricycle.

The museum's address is given as the corner of Jose Rizal Street and Juan Luna Street, while other sources also list it on Rizal Street in Barangay Garreta. Tell the driver "Juan Luna Museum" and he will know where to go.

The museum is mostly indoors, so the season matters little, but getting there is easier in the November–May dry season. March to May is hot in the daytime, so it is best to go when it opens in the morning.

In the June–October rainy season, typhoons and heavy rain are frequent and bus service may be unreliable. If rain is forecast, postpone or use a chartered vehicle. The museum is closed on Mondays, so Tuesday to Sunday is the safe choice.

NHCP museums, including this one, tend to be relatively quiet on weekday mornings. On days with school visits or weekend tourists the galleries get crowded, so just after opening is best. Around the New Year and Easter holidays all of Ilocos is crowded, so book transport and lodging early.

rows: The best time to tour the church, museum and beach together.
Visit early in the morning and spend midday indoors.
Travel is unreliable, so leave plenty of slack in your plans.

Badoc has little lodging, so most visitors stay in Laoag or Vigan and make a day trip. Half a day is enough to see the church and the museum.

You can easily find Ilocos foods such as bagnet (fried pork) and empanada at restaurants in town and along the road. There are not many large restaurants near the museum, so have lunch in the town center. At the beach, you can also rent a floating cottage to rest in. Prices differ by restaurant, so check first.

Badoc is the southernmost town in Ilocos Norte, about 39 km from Laoag and about 445 km from Manila, with a population of about 33,000 in 2024. The trip may seem long just for one museum, so it is more efficient to plan a southern Ilocos Norte day that combines Badoc Church, the beach and Badoc Island in the same town and continues on to Sinait Church. At the beach, check the wave conditions, and when renting a floating cottage ask the hourly rate first.
Many sources say the museum is closed on Mondays. Visit Tuesday to Sunday.
Operating hours differ by source, with opening at 8 or 9 a.m. and closing at 4 p.m. Going early in the morning to check is the safe choice.
Admission is free, but donations are said to be welcome. Give as you see fit.
The exhibit explanations may be mainly in English, so a translation app helps.
Reviews say there are many replicas, so visit in the spirit of following the brothers' story rather than expecting original works.
The original of Juan Luna's masterpiece, the Spoliarium, can be seen at the National Museum in Manila.
Seeing it together with Badoc Church fits comfortably in half a day.
If you travel as a family, telling your child briefly in advance who Juan Luna and Antonio Luna were makes the exhibits much more interesting.
Many NHCP-related museums are closed on Mondays and their hours sometimes change. Check local information before you visit so that you do not make a wasted trip.
Reviews say many exhibits are replicas. If you want to see original works, look for the National Museum in Manila separately.
Sources give the museum's address differently (Barangay 2, Garreta and so on), so ask your tricycle driver for it by name.
Dates such as Juan Luna's birth and baptism differ by source, so go by the museum's explanations.
It is hot at midday with little shade. Bring water and a hat.
It is a small provincial museum, and some exhibits may be closed for maintenance or events.
There is vehicle traffic on the road in front of the museum, so watch the road side when taking photos.
The parish church of St. John the Baptist, which enshrines the miraculous Virgin, close to the museum.
The church that enshrines the statue of Christ said to have come ashore from the same sea as the Badoc Virgin.
